problem_statement: The paper frames derivatives pricing and Value at Risk (VaR) computation as core quantitative-finance tasks that consume substantial computational resources in financial institutions. It also treats pricing problems as being solved either by Monte Carlo methods or by numerical PDE solvers, and focuses on quantum approaches intended to speed up those classical workflows.
problem_statement_quotes: Derivatives contracts are one of the fundamental pillars of modern financial markets and are routinely traded by both financial institutions and traders with a variety of objectives, such as financial risk hedging. For this reason, the fair valuation of financial derivatives, known as pricing, and the computation of various risk measures, such as the Value at Risk (VaR), have become two of the tasks that consume a great amount of computational resources in financial institutions.

Classically, the problems of derivatives pricing and the computation of VaR are mainly solved by means of Monte Carlo-simulation (MC) techniques or numerical algorithms for solving partial differential equations (PDE).
In this context, NExt ApplicationS of Quantum Computing (NEASQC) Use Case 5 (UC5) works on the de-velopment and evaluation of quantum algorithms for derivatives pricing and VaR problems.
classical_baseline: The paper treats Monte Carlo simulation as the de facto standard for pricing and VaR, while also noting finite-difference and other numerical PDE methods as another classical route for pricing problems. It explicitly contrasts quantum methods against classical Monte Carlo and classical PDE-based solvers.
classical_baseline_quotes: Classically, the problems of derivatives pricing and the computation of VaR are mainly solved by means of Monte Carlo-simulation (MC) techniques or numerical algorithms for solving partial differential equations (PDE).

The key advantage of MC technique is that it is easy to implement, very general and scales well with the dimension of the problem. Therefore, it has become the de facto standard by financial institutions to tackle both problems.

Another contender in the industry for solving pricing problems is through the direct solution of the PDE that arises from the derivatives pricing problem. Typically, Finite Differences methods are used to solve the PDE because the boundaries in pricing problems tend not to be very complex.
classical_difficulty: The paper says the classical Monte Carlo route is computationally expensive, even though it scales well and is general. It also says PDE methods are mainly attractive only for low-dimensional problems, while high-dimensional PDE approaches can suffer from exponentially small amplitudes when trying to read out prices from a quantum state, which the paper presents as a complexity issue in that setting.
classical_difficulty_quotes: fair valuation of financial derivatives, known as pricing, and the computation of various risk measures, such as the Value at Risk (VaR), have become two of the tasks that consume a great amount of computational resources in financial institutions.
These methods offer a faster convergence rate than MC methods for low-dimensional problems.
As an exponential number of grid points in the high dimensions leads to exponentially small amplitudes, it requires large time complexity to read it, thus loosing the potential quantum advantage.
business_stakes: The paper explicitly links derivatives pricing and VaR to financial institutions and risk hedging, and later says that the issues around noise and hardware limitations affect realistic financial applications. It also notes that near-term improvements may come from reduced energy consumption rather than speed.
business_stakes_quotes: Derivatives contracts are one of the fundamental pillars of modern financial markets and are routinely traded by both financial institutions and traders with a variety of objectives, such as financial risk hedging.

For this reason, the fair valuation of financial derivatives, known as pricing, and the computation of various risk measures, such as the Value at Risk (VaR), have become two of the tasks that consume a great amount of computational resources in financial institutions.

The issues raised by the presence of noise in quantum computer directly impact this use case. The reason for this is twofold. On the one hand, on the short term the high levels of noise prevents to implement efficient algorithms in NISQ technology.
In the near future, it means that the improvements that can be devised may come from a relevant decrease in energy consumption and not from a speed-wise improvement.
extraction_notes: Review/report paper with explicit motivation in executive summary and introduction; framing is broad and centered on pricing/VaR plus NISQ constraints.
